answer:
Let \(p_S(n)\) be the probability that, starting from a current total \(n\), the first perfect square reached is \(S\).

### Probability of stopping at 4
For target \(4\):
- \(p_4(4)=1\)
- \(p_4(1)=0\) and \(p_4(n)=0\) for \(n>4\) (except \(n=4\))

Then:
\[
p_4(3)=\frac{1}{6}
\]
\[
p_4(2)=\frac{p_4(3)+p_4(4)}{6}=\frac{\frac16+1}{6}=\frac{7}{36}
\]
\[
p_4(0)=\frac{p_4(1)+p_4(2)+p_4(3)+p_4(4)+p_4(5)+p_4(6)}{6}
=\frac{0+\frac{7}{36}+\frac16+1+0+0}{6}
=\frac{49}{216}
\]
So
\[
\boxed{\frac{49}{216}}
\]

### Probability of stopping at 9
For target \(9\), let \(q(n)\) be the probability of hitting \(9\) first from total \(n\). We have \(q(9)=1\), \(q(1)=q(4)=0\), and \(q(n)=0\) for \(n>9\).

Work backward:
\[
q(8)=\frac{1}{6}
\]
\[
q(7)=\frac{q(8)+q(9)}{6}=\frac{7}{36}
\]
\[
q(6)=\frac{q(7)+q(8)+q(9)}{6}=\frac{49}{216}
\]
\[
q(5)=\frac{q(6)+q(7)+q(8)+q(9)}{6}=\frac{343}{1296}
\]
\[
q(3)=\frac{q(5)+q(6)+q(7)+q(8)+q(9)}{6}=\frac{2401}{7776}
\]
\[
q(2)=\frac{q(3)+q(5)+q(6)+q(7)+q(8)}{6}=\frac{9031}{46656}
\]
Finally:
\[
q(0)=\frac{q(2)+q(3)+q(5)+q(6)}{6}
=\frac{46369}{279936}
\]
So
\[
\boxed{\frac{46369}{279936}}
\]

Thus the exact probabilities are:
\[
\boxed{\frac{49}{216} \text{ for stopping at } 4}
\]
\[
\boxed{\frac{46369}{279936} \text{ for stopping at } 9}
\]
